name: File-Oceanus
description: File-Oceanus is an oceanic world whose shallow continental shelves are covered with vast formations of razor-sharp coral analogues that file down anything that passes over them with industrial efficiency. The coral structures rise to within meters of the surface across enormous areas, creating navigational hazards for watercraft and defining the ecology of the planet. Between the coral shelves, deep channels of clear blue water support a marine ecosystem of extraordinary abundance, while perpetual storm systems churn the equatorial regions.

The ocean surface is deceptively calm between storms, a glassy expanse that conceals the razor shelves lurking just below. Bioluminescent organisms colonize the coral in such density that the shelves glow at night, creating a patchwork of light visible from orbit that maps the planet's submarine geography in ghostly blue-green. The air is heavy with moisture and the clean salt scent of productive ocean, and the storms, when they come, are magnificent displays of atmospheric power that can reshape the coral formations in a single violent night.

A derelict space station in orbit once served as the operational hub for a marine biology research initiative that lasted three decades before funding was cut. The station's databases contain the most comprehensive survey of the coral ecosystem ever compiled, data that is now degrading as the station's storage systems fail. A small research outpost on a floating platform continues the work with minimal staff, focused on the medicinal properties of compounds extracted from the coral organisms, several of which have shown remarkable promise in regenerative medicine.

File-Oceanus is a biological treasure trove whose value is increasingly recognized, but the razor coral makes large-scale harvesting dangerous and ecologically destructive. The derelict station's degrading databases represent an irreplaceable scientific resource that will be lost within years if not recovered. The coral ecosystem appears to be expanding, the shelves growing shallower and wider each decade, a trend that will eventually eliminate the deep channels and transform the planet's ecology in ways that cannot be predicted.
